chapter_summary:
Effective network troubleshooting is less about memorizing every possible problem and more about mastering a systematic, logical approach to problem-solving. When a network issue arises, the immediate urge might be to jump to conclusions or try random fixes. However, a structured methodology saves time, reduces frustration, and ensures that the root cause is identified and resolved, not just a symptom. One of the most fundamental frameworks for troubleshooting is the **OSI model**. By understanding which layer a problem is likely occurring at, you can narrow down your focus significantly. For instance, if users cannot access any external websites but can communicate with internal servers, the problem is likely at Layer 3 (Network) or Layer 7 (Application - specifically DNS resolution), rather than Layer 1 (Physical) or Layer 2 (Data Link).

Several systematic approaches guide you through the troubleshooting process. The **top-down approach** starts at the application layer (Layer 7) and works its way down. You might begin by checking if a specific application works, then if the web browser works, then if you can ping a remote host, and so on. This is often intuitive for end-users who experience problems at the application level. Conversely, the **bottom-up approach** starts at the physical layer (Layer 1) and works its way up. This is often preferred by network technicians when there's a suspected physical connectivity issue, such as "no link light" or a new device installation. You'd check cables, then switch ports, then IP addresses, and so forth. A highly effective method is **divide and conquer**, where you attempt to isolate the problem to a specific segment or device. For example, if half the users in a building can't connect, you might check the switch serving that half of the building. If a single user is affected, the problem is likely localized to their workstation or immediate connection.

Another crucial technique is **comparing configurations**. If a network component or service was working previously but is now failing, comparing its current configuration to a known good configuration (perhaps from a backup or a similar working device) can quickly highlight changes that might be causing the issue. This underscores the importance of maintaining accurate network documentation. Before even touching a device, **asking clarifying questions** is paramount. What exactly is the problem? When did it start? What changed recently? Who is affected? These questions help define the scope of the problem and provide valuable clues. Documentation, including network diagrams, IP address schemes, and configuration backups, serves as your map and compass during troubleshooting. Without it, you're navigating blind.

Let's look at some essential command-line tools. `ping` is your go-to for basic connectivity testing. It sends ICMP echo requests to a target host and listens for replies, indicating if the host is reachable and measuring latency. For example, `ping 8.8.8.8` tests connectivity to Google's DNS server. `tracert` (Windows) or `traceroute` (Linux/macOS) maps the path your packets take to a destination, showing each router (hop) along the way. This is invaluable for identifying where connectivity might be breaking down or where excessive latency is introduced. `ipconfig` (Windows) or `ifconfig` (Linux/macOS) displays your local network interface configuration, including IP address, subnet mask, default gateway, and DNS servers. This helps verify your device's network settings. Finally, `netstat` shows active network connections, listening ports, and routing tables, which can help identify if a service is running and listening on the correct port or if unexpected connections are present.

A common mistake in troubleshooting is failing to establish a baseline. Without knowing what "normal" looks like, it's difficult to identify what's abnormal. Always document your network's normal operating parameters, including latency, throughput, and error rates. Another pitfall is making multiple changes simultaneously. If you change five things at once and the problem resolves, you won't know which change fixed it, making future troubleshooting harder. Always make one change at a time and test the result. Finally, never assume. Always verify. Just because a link light is on doesn't mean the cable is good, and just because a service is configured doesn't mean it's running correctly.

screens.title: Network Troubleshooting Methodologies
screens.subtitle: A practical, structured approach to diagnosing and resolving network issues

narration.text: When a network problem appears, a calm, repeatable process saves time. In this lesson you will learn how to adopt systematic troubleshooting methodologies so you find root causes, not just temporary fixes. We’ll use the OSI model as a practical map to narrow where problems live, then learn three approaches — top-down, bottom-up, and divide-and-conquer — that guide what to check first. You’ll also see a concise toolset of command-line utilities: ping, tracert or traceroute, ipconfig or ifconfig, and netstat, and how they reveal connectivity, routing paths, interface settings, and active connections. Documentation and baselining are emphasized: keeping a record of normal behavior makes anomalies obvious, and asking focused clarifying questions defines the problem’s scope before you make changes. A brief hands-on scenario ties these ideas together so you can practice forming hypotheses from real command outputs. By the end, you’ll have a checklist-like mentality: verify, isolate, compare, and change one thing at a time. Think about a recent network glitch you saw — how might a structured approach have shortened your time to fix it?

keyIdea.title: Systematic troubleshooting beats guesswork
keyIdea.text: Use the OSI model, repeatable approaches, and simple command-line tools to isolate root causes, validate hypotheses, and preserve normal operation.

screens.title: The OSI model as a troubleshooting map
screens.subtitle: Use layers to focus tests and rule out broad classes of failures

narration.text: The OSI model is a seven-layer conceptual map that helps you ask targeted questions and run the right tests. When we say a problem is at a particular layer, we mean the core functionality for that layer is failing or behaving abnormally. For example, a physical layer issue might be a disconnected cable or a failed NIC — symptoms include total loss of connectivity and absent link lights. A network layer problem may allow local traffic but prevent routing to external networks; an application layer issue often shows as an inability to resolve domain names or a failing web application even though basic connectivity exists. Using layers reduces wasted effort: instead of randomly changing settings, you form a hypothesis such as, "Connectivity to IP addresses works, but hostnames do not," which points toward DNS and the application layer. A common misconception is to conflate symptoms and cause: just because a service fails doesn't mean the service itself is the cause; it might be a lower-layer problem. Practice: given a symptom, name the most likely OSI layer and one diagnostic command you would run to test it. That pairing — layer plus focused command — is the heart of efficient troubleshooting.

keyIdea.title: Layers guide focused tests
keyIdea.text: Map symptoms to OSI layers so you can choose commands that test the right functionality and avoid blind changes.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.1 › OSI model
Definition

The OSI model divides network functions into seven layers. Use it as a diagnostic map: start where symptoms indicate and run tests that prove or disprove a layer-specific hypothesis.

Layer 1 — Physical: cables, link lights
Layer 3 — Network: IP addressing, routing
Layer 2 — Data Link: MAC, switching
Layer 7 — Application: DNS, HTTP
Common misconception

Symptoms at the application layer don't prove an application fault. Always test lower layers first when evidence is ambiguous, because a broken link or misconfigured gateway can mimic application failures.

Practical pairing: layer → command
Test IP connectivity (Layer 3): ping <ip>
Trace route (Layer 3/4): tracert / traceroute <host>
Check interface settings (Layer 3): ipconfig / ifconfig
Confirm service endpoints (Layer 7): use DNS tests and application logs
Key Takeaway

Translate a symptom into a layer-based hypothesis and pick one command that verifies or rules it out. Repeat until the root cause is clear.

screens.title: Top-down troubleshooting
screens.subtitle: Start at the application layer and descend until the fault is found

narration.text: Top-down troubleshooting begins at the application layer because users most often notice application symptoms. The method is: verify the application first, then step downward through presentation, session, transport, network, data link, and physical layers as needed. For example, if a user reports that a web app won't load, you might first confirm the application itself works on another device or another user account. Next, check DNS resolution and browser settings. If hostname resolution succeeds but connections time out, use ping and traceroute to test connectivity and path hops. Continue descending until you find a layer that fails verification. This approach is efficient when the issue is user-facing and isolated to a single service. A common misconception is skipping down to lower layers immediately; that wastes time when the app or its configuration is the real problem. A disciplined top-down flow preserves configuration and avoids unnecessary hardware changes. As a practical test, describe each downward check you would perform when a single application on one machine reports failure, and note which command or UI you would use to verify each layer.

keyIdea.title: Start with the user's experience
keyIdea.text: Top-down is fastest when symptoms originate in applications; verify app behavior then move lower only when evidence points down.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.1 › Top-down
Step-by-step process
  1. Confirm the application error and reproduce it if possible.
  2. Check application settings and credentials.
  3. Verify DNS and hostname resolution.
  4. Test IP connectivity with ping.
  5. Use tracert/traceroute if reachability is partial.
  6. Inspect interface settings and physical connectivity last.
Example

If a single user's web browser reports 'page cannot be displayed', first test the site from another device, then run a DNS check, then ping an external IP. If DNS fails but ping to an IP succeeds, you likely have an application-layer DNS issue.

Supporting notes
  • Top-down maps naturally to user reports and application errors.
  • Start with low-risk tests and avoid making configuration changes too early.
  • If multiple users are affected, widen scope; do not confuse single-user app faults with network-wide failures.
Key Takeaway

Top-down testing reduces time-to-evidence for user-facing problems. Confirm app behavior before restructuring hardware or links.

screens.title: Bottom-up troubleshooting
screens.subtitle: Start at the physical layer and build upward to diagnose connectivity issues

narration.text: Bottom-up troubleshooting is a technician's favorite when a physical or link problem is suspected. Begin by verifying physical connectivity: check cables, connectors, link lights, and the network interface card. If physical indicators are fine, verify the data link layer — switch port configuration and VLAN membership — then confirm IP addressing and gateway settings at the network layer. For example, if a machine has no network activity and its link light is off, you start by replacing the cable or testing the patch panel port. After confirming link integrity, check ipconfig or ifconfig for a valid IP address and default gateway. If an IP is missing or autoconfiguration appears, work up the stack to DHCP and switch configuration. A common mistake is skipping physical checks because they seem trivial; this wastes time when the cable or port is the real culprit. The bottom-up method gives confidence that lower-layer fundamentals are solid before inspecting application-level behavior. Bottom-up troubleshooting means bottom-up ensures cables, ports, and ip basics are correct before higher-level diagnosis, saving time on physical faults.. In practical terms, start at the physical layer and build upward to diagnose connectivity issues. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Prove the fundamentals first
keyIdea.text: Bottom-up ensures cables, ports, and IP basics are correct before higher-level diagnosis, saving time on physical faults.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.1 › Bottom-up
Bottom-up steps
  1. Verify physical connectivity: link lights, cables, ports.
  2. Inspect Data Link: VLANs, MAC tables, switch port state.
  3. Confirm Network: IP address, subnet mask, default gateway.
  4. Test Transport and Application layers after basic connectivity is confirmed.
Example

A newly installed device shows no network. Checking the cable and switch port reveals no link light, indicating a physical fault. Replacing the cable restores link and allows the remainder of the stack to function.

Misconception to avoid

Don’t assume a green link light guarantees a good cable. Link may be present but with errors. Confirm with additional tests like ping and interface statistics if symptoms persist.

Key Takeaway

When physical symptoms exist, prove the lower layers first. Fixing a cable or port early prevents hours of wasted higher-level debugging.

screens.title: Divide and conquer
screens.subtitle: Isolate the fault to a segment, device, or user group

narration.text: Divide-and-conquer is an isolation strategy. Rather than testing the entire network, you reduce the problem space by splitting it into smaller parts and testing each independently. For instance, if half of the building’s users report loss of access to a resource, isolate by grouping users by switch, floor, or VLAN. Test the switch serving the affected group and compare it with a working switch. If a single user is affected, focus on workstation configuration, the immediate patch cable, and the local switch port. The approach applies to services too: compare the configuration of a failing device to a known-good device, which can reveal recent changes. A pitfall is changing both sides simultaneously during comparison; always change one variable at a time. The power of divide-and-conquer is speed — by shrinking the scope you reach evidence faster and avoid unnecessary wide-ranging changes. Practice thinking in halves: if something is wrong for many but not all, which boundary separates working from failing behavior? Divide and conquer means divide the environment to find boundaries between working and failing segments; use comparisons to spot configuration drift.. In practical terms, isolate the fault to a segment, device, or user group. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Shrink the problem space
keyIdea.text: Divide the environment to find boundaries between working and failing segments; use comparisons to spot configuration drift.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.1 › Divide and Conquer
Definition and strategy

Divide-and-conquer isolates faults by splitting the network or user population and testing each subset. It is most effective when some users work and others don't.

Segment isolation
Group affected users by switch or floor and test the border device to narrow the fault.
Device comparison
Compare a failing device’s config to a working one to reveal recent changes.
Single-user focus
If only one user is affected, limit tests to their workstation, cable, and nearest switch port.
Common mistake

Changing multiple variables during isolation hides which action actually fixed the problem. Make a single change, then test.

screens.title: Compare configurations & documentation
screens.subtitle: Why baselining and backups are your map and compass

narration.text: Comparing configurations is a high-leverage troubleshooting step. When a service that previously worked now fails, a side-by-side comparison of the current configuration and a known-good copy often reveals the change that introduced the fault. Configuration backups, network diagrams, and IP address inventories are documentation that speed this comparison. Baselining means recording expected normal operating metrics — typical latency, throughput, and error rates — so you can identify deviations quickly. In practice, before changing a device, capture its current config as a snapshot and label it with date and context. Then, if your change creates side effects, you can roll back. A common pitfall is poor documentation: without diagrams and baselines, you spend time rediscovering what should already be known. Keep notes of DHCP ranges, gateway addresses, and DNS servers so command-line outputs lead directly to answers. Good documentation shortens incident time dramatically and prevents guesswork. Compare configurations & documentation means maintain configuration snapshots and baselines to rapidly detect change and compare current state to a known-good reference.. In practical terms, why baselining and backups are your map and compass. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Documentation speeds diagnosis
keyIdea.text: Maintain configuration snapshots and baselines to rapidly detect change and compare current state to a known-good reference.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.1 › Compare Configurations
Practical steps
  • Capture current configuration and label with date/time and context.
  • Store known-good configs for similar devices and environments.
  • Use documentation to map IP ranges, DNS servers, and gateway addresses.
Analogy

Think of a baseline like a photograph of a working state. If a later problem appears, comparing the new photo to the baseline quickly shows what changed.

Why it matters

Good documentation reduces time spent guessing. When a configuration drift causes failure, comparison points you to the precise setting that changed, speeding remediation and enabling reliable rollbacks.

screens.title: Using ping and tracert/traceroute
screens.subtitle: Verify reachability, measure latency, and reveal hop-by-hop routes

narration.text: Ping and tracert (or traceroute) are fundamental diagnostic tools. Ping sends ICMP echo requests to a target and reports replies and round-trip time; it lets you know whether a host is reachable and gives a latency measure. Tracert or traceroute shows each router hop along the path and the latency to each hop, which helps localize where a route fails or where latency spikes occur. For example, if you can ping 8.8.8.8 but pinging a domain name fails, that suggests DNS resolution issues rather than routing faults. If tracert shows a timeout at a specific hop, that hop may be dropping ICMP or suffering congestion. A common misunderstanding is treating a single failed hop in traceroute as absolute evidence of end-to-end failure; some routers deprioritize or block traceroute packets while still forwarding traffic. Use these tools together: ping to confirm reachability, traceroute to localize path issues, and then combine results with other evidence like ipconfig output to form a hypothesis. Using ping and tracert/traceroute means start with ping for reachability; use tracert/traceroute to find where along the path time or failure appears.. In practical terms, verify reachability, measure latency, and reveal hop-by-hop routes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Ping then trace
keyIdea.text: Start with ping for reachability; use tracert/traceroute to find where along the path time or failure appears.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.1 › Ping & Traceroute
What ping shows

Reachability and round-trip latency to an IP. Use it to confirm basic connectivity and approximate performance.

What tracert/traceroute shows

Each router hop along the path and the response time for each hop. Use it to find the hop where delays or failures begin.

Command examples
ping 8.8.8.8
tracert google.com    (Windows)
traceroute google.com (Linux/macOS)
Interpretation tips
  • If ping to IP works but ping to a name fails, suspect DNS or application-layer resolution.
  • Asterisks or timeouts on a traceroute hop may indicate ICMP being deprioritized, not necessarily end-to-end failure.
  • Use multiple tests and times to avoid transient misleading results.
Key Takeaway

Ping gives a yes/no reachability check; traceroute localizes where along the path latency or failures appear. Use both to form a precise hypothesis.

screens.title: ipconfig / ifconfig and netstat
screens.subtitle: Inspect interface settings, routing, and active connections

narration.text: ipconfig and ifconfig display your interface settings — IP address, subnet mask, default gateway, and DNS servers — which are essential to validate before deeper testing. Netstat lists active network connections, listening ports, and routing table entries. Together, these commands tell you whether your host has a valid address, which gateway it will use, and whether services are listening where you expect. For example, ipconfig /all on Windows shows configured DNS servers; if you see only an internal DNS that is unresponsive while ping to an IP works, DNS is suspect. Netstat can reveal unexpected listening services or suspicious established connections that might distract from the real network issue. A common mistake is to assume the configuration is correct without checking: always capture the interface output and include it in notes. Practice reading sample outputs: identify the IPv4 address, default gateway, and DNS entries, then form the next test based on those findings. ipconfig / ifconfig and netstat means use ipconfig/ifconfig to confirm addressing and netstat to inspect active connections before making higher-level changes.. In practical terms, inspect interface settings, routing, and active connections. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Verify host configuration
keyIdea.text: Use ipconfig/ifconfig to confirm addressing and netstat to inspect active connections before making higher-level changes.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.1 › ipconfig / netstat
ipconfig / ifconfig — what to look for
  • IPv4 Address and Subnet Mask: ensure they are in expected range.
  • Default Gateway: necessary for routing beyond local subnet.
  • DNS Servers: critical for name resolution.
netstat — what to inspect

Look for listening ports for expected services and unusual established connections that could indicate misconfiguration or unrelated problems.

Sample outputs

Ethernet adapter Ethernet:

   Subnet Mask . . . . . . . . . . . : 255.255.255.0
   Default Gateway . . . . . . . . . : 192.168.1.1
   DNS Servers . . . . . . . . . . . : 192.168.1.1, 8.8.8.8

# Example netstat partial
Active Connections

  TCP    192.168.1.100:50524  172.217.0.46:443     ESTABLISHED
Key Takeaway

Capture and save interface and connection outputs before changing settings. These snapshots are vital for comparison and rollback decisions.

screens.title: Scenario: Diagnosing DNS vs routing
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step terminal workflow when external sites fail but internal access works

narration.text: You are presented with a common report: a user can reach internal file shares but cannot access external websites. A structured terminal workflow helps you confirm whether this is DNS, routing, or something else. First, capture the IP configuration using ipconfig /all or ifconfig; note the IP, gateway, and DNS servers. Next, ping the default gateway to confirm the local router responds. Then ping an external IP such as 8.8.8.8. If ping to the IP succeeds but ping to a hostname like google. com fails, DNS resolution is probably failing. To further localize, run tracert or traceroute to the hostname and to an external IP; if traceroute to an IP traverses correctly but traceroute to a name fails early, that again points to DNS. Form a hypothesis, such as 'client has a valid route to the internet but DNS servers are misconfigured or unreachable.' Record the hypothesis, then check the DNS server listed in the interface output and test DNS service from that server if possible. Always end by documenting findings and any changes made. Scenario: Diagnosing DNS vs routing means use ipconfig, ping, and traceroute in sequence to distinguish between routing and dns failures and form a testable hypothesis.. In practical terms, step-by-step terminal workflow when external sites fail but internal access works. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Follow the evidence
keyIdea.text: Use ipconfig, ping, and traceroute in sequence to distinguish between routing and DNS failures and form a testable hypothesis.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.1 › Lab: DNS vs Routing
Step-by-step terminal workflow
  1. Run ipconfig /all or ifconfig and note IP, gateway, and DNS.
  2. Ping the default gateway: ping <gateway_ip>.
  3. Ping an external IP: ping 8.8.8.8.
  4. Ping a hostname: ping google.com.
  5. If IP ping works but name ping fails, run tracert/traceroute for further evidence.
Example expected outputs
# If ping 8.8.8.8 succeeds but ping google.com fails
# Hypothesis: DNS resolution failing
# Next steps: verify DNS server listed in ipconfig, test DNS service, and check DNS server reachability
Wrap-up

Document your findings, state the hypothesis and tests you ran, and make only one configuration change at a time when attempting remediation. Capture outputs so you can roll back if needed.

screens.title: Common troubleshooting mistakes and how to avoid them
screens.subtitle: Practice discipline: baselines, single changes, and verification

narration.text: Troubleshooting errors often stem not from technical ignorance but from poor process. Three common mistakes are: not having a baseline, making multiple changes at once, and assuming symptoms equal cause. Without a baseline, you lack a reference to decide what changed. Making several configuration changes at once breaks the feedback loop — you cannot tell which action produced the effect. And assuming a symptom's visible effect is the root cause leads to incorrect fixes. Avoid these mistakes by recording normal operating metrics, taking snapshots before changing devices, and making one change at a time followed by validation. Another practical safeguard is asking clarifying questions to define scope and context before touching the network. For example, ask who is affected, what changed recently, and when the problem began. These steps slow you down slightly, but they dramatically reduce the chance of introducing new faults and make your fixes repeatable and auditable. Common troubleshooting mistakes and how to avoid them means keep baselines, change one thing at a time, and verify results to avoid compounding faults during troubleshooting.. In practical terms, practice discipline: baselines, single changes, and verification. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Process discipline prevents errors
keyIdea.text: Keep baselines, change one thing at a time, and verify results to avoid compounding faults during troubleshooting.

content.html:

Mistake vs Fix
No baseline
Capture normal state metrics and configs
Multiple changes at once
Change one item, then test and document
Assuming symptom is root cause

Clarifying questions
  • What exactly isn't working, and for whom?
  • When did it start, and what changed recently?
  • Is the problem reproducible and limited to a segment?
Key Takeaway

A disciplined process avoids guesswork. Document and verify each step so your fixes are reliable and reversible.

screens.title: Forming a hypothesis and testing it
screens.subtitle: Turn command outputs into a clear, testable theory

narration.text: A hypothesis links evidence to an actionable cause. After collecting command outputs, state a clear hypothesis such as, 'The client can reach external IPs but cannot resolve domain names; therefore DNS is failing.' From that hypothesis derive a single next test or change, for example, 'Change the client DNS to 8.8.8.8 and re-test name resolution.' Execute the test and observe results. If the test proves the hypothesis, document the fix. If not, use the evidence to refine your hypothesis and choose the next test. This process converts ad-hoc tinkering into a repeatable scientific workflow: observe, hypothesize, test, analyze, and document. A common misconception is treating every test as final; instead, treat each test as an experiment that informs the next step. Practice writing a short hypothesis after running ipconfig, ping, and traceroute on the hands-on scenario. That concise statement will guide your remediation and make post-incident notes clear to your team. Module 06 › Chapter 6.1 › Hypothesis Testing
Workflow
  1. Collect evidence with ipconfig/ping/traceroute.
  2. Write a concise hypothesis linking evidence to cause.
  3. Design and run one test to validate the hypothesis.
  4. Document results and next steps.
Example hypothesis

"Client reaches external IPs but cannot resolve hosts; DNS servers configured on the client are unreachable, causing name resolution failure."

Example test

Change the client's DNS server temporarily to a known public resolver, then re-run ping to a hostname. If it resolves, the hypothesis is supported; if not, refine the hypothesis and continue testing.

Key Takeaway

Hypotheses make troubleshooting scientific and communicable. Keep tests minimal and document outcomes for team visibility and rollback capability.

screens.subtitle: Core ideas to carry into your next troubleshooting incident

narration.text: These are the essential concepts to retain. Use the OSI model as your diagnostic map to target tests. Apply top-down when the problem is application-facing and bottom-up when physical connectivity is suspected. Use divide-and-conquer to isolate the fault to a device or segment quickly. Maintain baselines and configuration snapshots so changes and anomalies are obvious. Run a small, essential set of commands—ping, tracert/traceroute, ipconfig/ifconfig, and netstat—to collect evidence before making changes. Always ask focused clarifying questions to define scope and never change multiple things at once; make one change, then verify. These habits shorten incident time, make fixes safer, and create a reliable record for future incidents. Keep this short checklist in mind next time you’re called to investigate a network issue. screens.subtitle: Three short reminders to use on every incident

narration.text: Keep these three reminders in mind. First, evidence before action: gather command outputs and document the current state before changing anything. Second, one change at a time: this preserves the causal link between action and outcome. Third, compare to a baseline or a known-good configuration to spot drift quickly. These simple practices reduce incidents, speed diagnosis, and make fixes reversible. They also make your work teachable: clear notes and repeatable steps let teammates reproduce and validate your remediation. Carry this short checklist into every call you take.
